how_to_read: 1. Read the head first: the first 33 lines hold manifest, essence and routing (Read limit=33, or jq '{manifest, essence, routing}' rare-cloud-haiku.metadump.json).
2. Pick the route for your job and run its jq: jq '<routing[i].jq>' rare-cloud-haiku.metadump.json
3. Also pull the anti-keywords and review prompts (checks) for your scope: jq '.anti_keywords, .checks' rare-cloud-haiku.metadump.json
4. Look up any term (lowercase): jq '.index["<term>"]' rare-cloud-haiku.metadump.json  -> hits give id + path; not_meant lists senses to avoid.
5. Grep works too: every entry is one line, so grep -n '<word>' rare-cloud-haiku.metadump.json returns whole entries.

essence.one_sentence: Rare clouds reach a haiku through what the eye can name and place, and the reading of rare that is chosen decides which seen thing carries it.
essence.summary: Four readings of rare sit side by side with no verdict among them: a sighting of a named cloud or its light, the rarity itself, a sky that seldom shows its clouds, and a precious moment that will not come back. Each takes a different thing to name.

formula.full: one combination among several: a named cloud, the hour and light that show it, one cut, and a second image set across the cut
formula.essential: one seen thing set across one cut from a second
options: an unnamed sight described by its look, with no hour
a sound at the sighting (ice underfoot, wind over a ridge) in place of a look, or beside it
a season-free form, with no kigo and no natural image of the season

roles.hour and light, or none: the time and the colour, when the poem sets them
roles.cut: the pause that lets the reader join the images

angles.text: A lens-shaped cloud holds over a ridge while the air runs through it; the still shape is the image, and the wind is left to the reader.
A faint pale streak on a deep blue sky after dusk, found only by searching the sky above the horizon; the search is part of the sighting.
Mother-of-pearl colour stays on a cloud after the sun has gone below the horizon, and fades within a short window.
Only the thin edge of a cloud takes a colour, and only for a while; what is small is the place where the rarity shows.
An autumn dusk is an image the haiku tradition already knows; the season and the hour arrive together in one image.

llm_brief.text:
On the table: the user's words, quoted: 'a haiku about rare clouds'. Rare has four readings side by side: a sighting of a named cloud or its light; the rarity itself, how seldom such clouds come and the luck of seeing one; a sky that seldom shows its clouds; a precious moment that will not come back. Named clouds, one sighting each: nacreous, a winter stratospheric ice cloud, pearly pink and green through dark grey, about 10 to 30 km up, coloured after sunset; lenticular, lens-shaped, holding its place over a ridge while the air streams through it; noctilucent, the highest clouds, about 80 to 85 km up, faint blue-white streaks on a deep blue sky with stars still showing; cloud iridescence, colour on the edges of thin cloud. Clip timing: over 9.5 s the streaks barely move; a dark band crosses early, about the first 2.3 s. Haiku craft: kigo (a word or image that fixes the season), kireji (the cut: dash, line break or grammatical break), juxtaposition of two concrete images, shasei (sketching what was seen). Autumn dusk (aki no yuugure) is a favoured haiku image.
Ways in, none marked as the default: the lens that stands still over a ridge. Colour that stays on a cloud after the sun has left the ground. A faint streak across a deep blue sky, found only by searching. The thin edge of a cloud taking one colour for a while. An autumn dusk, where season and hour arrive in one image. The quiet of ice beside the look of the cloud.
Dials: form, three lines, in English short-long-short or a 5-7-5 count (5, 7, 5 for illustration). Cut mark: a dash, a line break, or a shift between the two images. Subject: a named cloud (lenticular, nacreous, noctilucent, an iridescent edge) or an unnamed sight described by its look. Season: a season word or natural image, or none. Hour: dusk, after sunset, low sun, dawn, or no hour. Distance: near enough to name the edge, far enough to see the whole shape.
Worn paths: the usual cloud is soft, white, fluffy or cotton; fresher: a lens over a ridge, or colour on a thin edge. The usual verb is drifting; fresher: holding still, or thinning. The usual mood word is dreamy, ethereal or ghostly; fresher: a colour you can name, such as mother-of-pearl pink. The usual last line is a moral or a silver lining; fresher: end on the second image. The usual move with rare is a verdict; fresher: let the seen thing, or the moment, carry the rarity. Filler such as stunning or breathtaking adds nothing; fresher: the one detail the eye noticed.
Open, with defaults only where a parameter is needed to go on: the language (English, unless another is named); the strictness of the form (English short-long-short, or a 5-7-5 count); the season (none unless one is set); the observer (a present sighting, a memory, or someone else seeing it).

ak-fluffy-cloud.instead: a named type seen by its edge or shape: a lens stood over a ridge, colour on a thin edge
ak-fluffy-cloud.text: The default cloud is soft, white and round. A rare cloud is seen by a feature the eye can name.

ak-stock-mood.instead: a colour you can name: mother-of-pearl pink, a bluish glow after dusk, or edge colour on thin cloud
ak-stock-mood.text: Mood words stand in for the look of the cloud.

ak-silver-lining.instead: the underside lit by a low sun, or one edge catching a colour the rest of the sky lacks
ak-silver-lining.text: A hopeful turn added to the image. The sighting does not need it.

ak-drifting.instead: a cloud that stays put: a lens held over a ridge while air streams through, or a wisp that thins
ak-drifting.text: The default verb for clouds. Some rare clouds hold still, which is the more exact motion to write.

ak-closing-moral.instead: end on the second image and stop: the cut lets the reader join the two
ak-closing-moral.text: A last line that says what the image means closes the cut and the reader's part.

ak-rare-said.instead: let the seen thing carry the rarity: a colour only at dusk, a cloud the eye must search for
ak-rare-said.text: Calling the cloud rare in the poem tells the reader what the image should have shown.

ak-rare-as-valuable.instead: precious as a sighting that will not come back, not as goods
ak-rare-as-valuable.text: Rare read as worth or price. The precious reading in the request is about a moment that will not repeat.

ak-clouds-not-computing.excluded_sense: cloud computing; 'in the clouds' as vagueness
ak-clouds-not-computing.instead: visible water-droplet clouds in the sky
ak-clouds-not-computing.text: The computing sense of cloud. The request means the sky.

ak-rare-underdone.excluded_sense: underdone (rare meat); thin-air rare unless chosen
ak-rare-underdone.instead: uncommon, sparse, or precious cloud: one of the readings in cl-rare-readings

ak-noise-intensifiers.instead: the thing the eye caught: a colour, an edge, the hour, or the cloud's shape
ak-noise-intensifiers.text: Filler words with no image in them; see worn_paths.wp-noise.

k-named-cloud.text: Does the poem name one cloud or light by a shape, an edge or a colour the eye can check, or describe an unnamed sight by its look?

test.spec: one named cloud or light, with a shape, edge or colour; or an unnamed sight described by its look

k-rare-not-said.text: Does the poem let the seen thing carry the rarity, without calling the cloud rare?

test.spec: no judgement word for rarity in the poem

k-no-fluffy.text: Does any line describe the cloud as fluffy, cotton, puffy or pillowy?

k-no-stock-mood.text: Are dreamy, ethereal or ghostly standing in for a colour or a shape?

k-no-moral.text: Does the last line say what the image means, closing the cut for the reader?

test.spec: the last line ends on the second image

k-no-silver-lining.text: Is a hopeful turn tacked onto the image?

k-cut-marked.text: Is there one cut, marked by a dash, a line break or a shift, between two concrete images?

k-hour-light.text: Does the poem place the sighting in an hour or a light, such as dusk, after sunset or low sun, or leave the hour unnamed?

test.spec: an hour or a light that shows the cloud, or no hour at all

k-colour-named.text: How is the colour seen: could a reader match it by eye, or is it given as a mood?

test.spec: a colour a reader could match by eye, or a shape or edge without colour

k-seen-not-invented.text: Is the image written as it was seen, rather than invented for the poem?

test.spec: details that could be observed at the sighting

k-motion-still.text: If the cloud is a noctilucent streak, does it stay still rather than drift?

test.spec: a still verb such as holds, hangs or thins

k-form-count.text: Does the poem keep the form the user chose, three lines with the chosen count?

test.spec: three lines; syllables per line as chosen (5-7-5, or short-long-short)

oq-language.text: In what language is the poem written?
oq-language.impact: every line and the syllable count
oq-language.resolve: ask the user, or keep English as the prompt's language

oq-form.text: Strict 5-7-5 syllables, or English short-long-short lines with one cut?
oq-form.default: English short-long-short lines with one cut
oq-form.impact: line lengths and the rhythm of the cut
oq-form.resolve: ask the user, or use the default

oq-season.text: Which season, if any, does the poem carry?
oq-season.default: no season word unless one is set; the kigo options stay side by side
oq-season.impact: whether a season word or natural image appears
oq-season.resolve: ask the user, or leave the season unstated

request._about: The user's words, verbatim. The only shard that mints user_stated.
request._notes: Two-way words: 'rare' (uncommon by type, by moment, sparse or thin, or precious) and 'clouds' (sky clouds, not cloud computing). 'haiku' is the poem form here, not a model name. Language of the poem and season are not stated.

req-haiku.text: The requested form is a haiku.

visual_reference._about: Rare cloud images and the noctilucent clip, found online and looked at (lite moodboard and video). Descriptions are visual observations of the collected files; colour values are pixel samples from the photos, not print specs. Timings are frame-diff measures at 4 fps, so durations are +/- 250 ms.

vis-fallstreak-holes.text: A flat sheet of small rounded cloud elements with two clean circular gaps, the edges of each gap curling inward.
signals: round hole with a soft hooked rim
behaviors: The hole opens where cloud droplets have frozen and fallen out, so the rim curls toward the hole
Holes sit in a sheet that otherwise looks unchanged
vis-fallstreak-holes.note: CC BY-SA 4.0 stated on the Commons page: share-alike applies to derivatives.

vis-mammatus-underside.term: mammatus pouches under a storm sheet
vis-mammatus-underside.text: Dark grey, almost black-and-white panorama of rounded pouches hanging from a low cloud deck over a dark ridge.
signals: tree silhouettes on a flat horizon
behaviors: Pouches read as hanging because light comes from the side and the underside stays darker
vis-mammatus-underside.note: CC BY-NC 3.0 stated: non-commercial only. A GFDL alternative is listed on the page. Flag before commercial use.

vis-lenticular-stack.term: lenticular cloud as stacked lens layers
vis-lenticular-stack.text: A lens-shaped cloud, flat-based and smooth-edged, stacked in pale curved layers that thin toward the rim.
behaviors: The layers stay still while the air moves through them, so the shape holds in wind
vis-lenticular-stack.note: NASA APOD page credits J. D. Rufo; the page declares no licence in the pick. Use the credit line.

vis-nacreous-irisation.text: Thin wavy wisps, pearly pastel bands of pink, green and gold through dark grey, lit from below the horizon. Gallery frames show the band over pine silhouettes.
signals: iridescent bands on a grey-violet sky
behaviors: Irisation shows only where the sun is below the horizon, so the sky around it is already dark
Bands follow the wind shear, so the wisps read as flowing lines rather than puffs
The clouds read as a thin colour band, not as a white mass
vis-nacreous-irisation.note: Antarctica photo: CC BY 2.0 stated on the Commons page; attribution required. Spaceweather photos: no licence stated on the page.

vis-noctilucent-streaks.text: Faint blue-white streaks, fine and diagonal, across a deep blue night sky above town lights and dark trees.
signals: amber glow low on the horizon
behaviors: The streaks are dim against the dark sky, so they show best well after sunset with the horizon still lit
Streaks stay separate with dark gaps between them, rather than merging into one sheet
Brightest parts sit against the darkest part of the sky
vis-noctilucent-streaks.principle: A faint, fine-streaked cloud shows only where the sky around it is already dark.
vis-noctilucent-streaks.note: Video CC BY 4.0 stated on the Commons page (from discover).

vid-clip.text: 9.5 s night time-lapse, 1280x720, over a rail yard and town lights. No captions.

segments.note: dark band crosses the sky; too short to classify easing
streak change stays near the noise floor

vid-motion-timing.text: The only large change is a dark band across the sky in the first 2.3 s. After that the streaks barely change for about 7 s.

vid-f4.text: Thin pale blue-white streaks run diagonally across a deep blue night sky. Stars show. A faint amber band sits low behind trees, a tower and streetlights.

vid-f2.text: A dark wedge fills the upper left of the frame. No streaks are visible in that part of the sky.

lf-nlc-motion.text: Over the 9.5 s clip the streaks hardly move. The visible change is a dark band that crosses the sky early on, plus the light of a passing train.
behaviors: Between about 2.3 s and the end, frame-to-frame change stays near the noise floor
Within a time-lapse, drift of a high cloud is too slow to read in a short clip
lf-nlc-motion.principle: A short clip shows the timelapse steps and whatever crosses the frame, not the slow drift of the cloud itself.

craft._about: The form, the count, the cut, the distance between images and the season word: the parts a writer sets by hand. Builds on the primer's craft_principles and haiku_practice (builds_on), it does not restate them.

options._about: options, not requirements: decision points where the prompt is silent, each with its tradeoff

opt-named-or-unnamed.text: A named cloud (lenticular, mammatus, nacreous) gives the reader a term to check; an unnamed sight described by its look keeps the poem open and avoids a field-guide tone.

opt-count-or-rhythm.text: A strict count shows craft but can pad the lines; short-long-short with a cut reads more naturally in English.

opt-cut-mark.term: dash, line break or image shift
opt-cut-mark.text: A dash marks the cut plainly; a line break lets the layout do the work; an image shift needs no mark but asks the most of the juxtaposition.

sc-transfer.text: Options for the poem: the stacked bands as the image, the unseen mountain wave as the cause, or the far-off look as the view.
sc-transfer.principle: The mechanism can stay offstage while the layers do the seeing.

opt-kigo-or-image.term: Japanese season word or English natural image
opt-kigo-or-image.text: A kigo keeps the tradition but needs a reader who knows it; an English natural image carries the season with no glossary; no season word at all keeps the poem season-free.

opt-sighting-setting.term: hour and sound of the sighting
opt-sighting-setting.text: Options for the setting: an hour (dusk, after sunset, low sun, dawn, or none) and a sound (ice, wind over a ridge, a frozen lake's quiet), which can stand in for the look or sit beside it.
behaviors: Where the light is the rarity, the hour does the work
A poem with no hour is also an option
A sound can stand in for the look of the cloud, or sit beside it

cr-count.text: Japanese haiku counts sound units (on) in 5-7-5; English practice counts syllables loosely or uses a short-long-short shape.
behaviors: Strict 5-7-5 in English tends to pad filler words into lines
Counting by vowel sound catches most drift; read the line aloud for the rest
cr-count.principle: A count is a choice; when one is used, state it and keep it.

bad: silent final e counted as a syllable

cr-cut.text: Show the cut with a dash, a line break or a shift of image, and keep the same mark throughout.
behaviors: A dash after line one makes the second image answer the first
A line break after line two lets the last line land alone and sharp
cr-cut.principle: The cut is where the reader's part of the poem begins.
signals: a visible break after line one or line two

cp-kigo.text: A word or natural image that tells the reader which season the experience happened in.
properties: natural image that fixes the season
behaviors: A rare cloud seen in a particular season carries the season through its image, not through a label
A season word in line one sets the time before the cloud appears
Frost on glass or a cold blue hour carries the season without the word
cp-kigo.principle: A season gives the image a time as well as a place.
signals: no two season cues that disagree

cp-kireji-cut.text: A cut marks a pause between two parts of a haiku; English haiku may use dash, line break or grammatical break in its place.
behaviors: A cut after the cloud line lets the sky line stand as a second image
Without a cut the poem reads as one flat sentence
cp-kireji-cut.principle: The cut makes two images meet and leaves the reader to join them.
signals: a pause or break after one of the three lines

cp-juxtaposition.text: Two concrete images set across the cut with no connecting verb; the link is left to the reader.
behaviors: A rare cloud beside a plain observed detail from the same moment: the link is felt
A cloud beside a general or distant image: the link is lost unless the cut is sharp
If the two images are too close the poem explains itself
cp-juxtaposition.principle: Close enough to touch, far enough that the reader has to cross the gap.
signals: two concrete images with no explaining word between them

cp-shasei.text: Shasei is direct observation written down as it was seen, not invented imagery.
behaviors: A sighting of a cloud is written from what the eye saw: its edge, its colour, the time
Shasei used as a flat list of facts reads as dull, which is the common complaint
cp-shasei.principle: Look first; the image comes from what was seen, not from what the poet expects to see.
signals: a detail a reader could check at the same hour and place

cr-form.text: Three lines with one cut that splits the poem into two images, the first and the second.
behaviors: Short, long, short lines give the common English shape
A cut after line one leaves lines two and three as one image; after line two, line one stands alone
A strict 5-7-5 in English tends to pad or cram the lines
cr-form.principle: The form is the three lines and the cut; the count is a choice, and a stated one if used.

hp-check-against-request.term: check a haiku against the request
hp-check-against-request.text: Check the form, the season cue, the cut, and whether the cloud and the chosen reading of rare are still present.
behaviors: If the rare cloud has been swapped for a general sky, the poem has drifted from the request
A season word that does not match the cloud's season needs a revision, not an explanation
hp-check-against-request.principle: A revision that keeps the cloud and the cut is usually enough.

clouds._about: Options, not requirements. The readings of 'rare' for clouds, the verified pool indexed by reading (cloud_types and the scrape jobs hold the entries), and the sensory detail of a sighting. Nothing here picks a cloud for the poem.

cl-pool-by-reading.text: The verified candidates in cloud_types, grouped by the reading each serves. Several readings have only two or three, so a research pass should add more before the pool is used as a menu.
properties: uncommon moment: nacreous, iridescence on thin edges, plus the sightings in ns-hour-light and the APOD lenticular scrape
sparse or thin: noctilucent, nacreous by day
behaviors: Sparse or thin and precious each have two verified candidates, below the target of more than two per reading

rc-noctilucent.reading: sparse or thin: little of it, very high; precious: seen only in summer twilight
rc-noctilucent.text: The highest clouds in the atmosphere, about 80-85 km up, lit by sun long after sunset.
properties: shines while lower clouds show dark
amber band low on the horizon after sunset
behaviors: Seen against the twilight arch on long summer nights
Faint overhead, bright when edge-on to the observer
The horizon glow stays amber while the sky overhead is already dark blue
signals: a luminous sheet in the northern night sky
bluish glow after dusk in summer
pale streaks on deep blue with stars

rc-lenticular.reading: uncommon type: a named lens shape that stays in place while air moves through it
rc-lenticular.text: Lens-shaped wave cloud that stands still over a mountain-induced gravity wave while the air streams through it.
behaviors: Forms downwind of mountain ranges as wind rolling off the land makes the air bob up and down
Moist layers saturate one at a time, so clear air stays between the sheets
Holds still while air passes through; slow drift in other clouds usually means distance
rc-lenticular.principle: The cloud is made by air moving up and down, not by air moving across.
signals: a stack of smooth lenses over a ridge

rc-iridescence-edge.reading: uncommon moment: the light on ordinary cloud that is itself rare
rc-iridescence-edge.text: Localized colour on the edges of thin tropospheric cloud, from diffraction of sunlight.
behaviors: Strongest when the sun is low and lights cloud from below

ns-colour-shift.reading: precious: a sighting that will not come back
ns-colour-shift.text: Captions describe the colour as building and then fading, from pale and mutating to vivid to a last flash of orange.
properties: bright orange at the last rays
behaviors: The colour peaks after the sun is down, not while it is up
The final colour is one brief flash before the cloud disappears
signals: colour that strengthens as the sky darkens

ns-sensory.reading: uncommon by moment: a walk by a frozen lake at dusk
ns-sensory.text: The one sensory detail captions give beyond colour is the reflection on ice.
behaviors: Looking down at the frozen lake shows the cloud colour a second time
Cold and quiet are implied by the setting, not described
signals: a still lake holding the sky

ns-caveat.term: how much to trust these captions
ns-caveat.text: All of this is secondhand: photographers describing their own sightings, with camera and editing notes. The page gives no measurements of colour or time.
behaviors: Use the captions as the feel of a sighting, not as fact about the cloud

cl-rare-readings.text: 'Rare' for clouds can mean an uncommon type, an uncommon moment, a sparse or thin cloud, or a precious sighting. Each reading points to a different poem.

readings.in_practice: A named form seen seldom. Exemplar: lenticular, a lens-shaped cloud that holds still over a ridge while air streams through it (rc-lenticular).
signals: a stack of smooth lenses over a ridge

readings.in_practice: The right hour, place and light make ordinary cloud rare. Exemplar: colour on thin cloud edges (rc-iridescence-edge). Nacreous cloud after sunset in mid-January, lasting about an hour (ns-hour-light).
signals: colour after the sun drops below the horizon

readings.in_practice: Little cloud, or very high or very thin. Exemplar: noctilucent, extremely thin and tenuous, about 80-85 km up (rc-noctilucent). Nacreous by day looks pale and cirrus-like (rc-nacreous).
signals: streaks with dark gaps between them

readings.in_practice: A sighting that will not come back. Exemplar: nacreous, whose colour peaks and then fades in minutes (ns-colour-shift). Noctilucent is seen on long summer twilights (rc-noctilucent).

cl-lead-nitric-psc.term: nitric acid and water polar stratospheric cloud
cl-lead-nitric-psc.text: A thin yellowish veil, duller than nacreous cloud, forming below about -78 C in high-latitude winter. Lead from a WMO page, seen only as a summary: check before use.

ns-hour-light.term: hour and light of the sighting
ns-hour-light.reading: uncommon by moment: the right hour, place and light
ns-hour-light.text: One photographer's sighting, near Oslo on the evening of January 20th: the sun set about 16.00 and the show lasted about an hour. One sighting among several; other hours and places are open.
properties: start a couple of hours before sunset
behaviors: The clouds catch light after the sun has set below the horizon
The window is short: roughly an hour from first colour to last
signals: low light from below the horizon

rc-nacreous.reading: precious: a sighting that will not come back; uncommon moment
rc-nacreous.text: Winter stratospheric ice cloud, seen after sunset. One source calls a sighting from southern England a once in a lifetime sighting; that place is one example, not the usual one.
behaviors: Forms only where the stratosphere drops below about -85 C, often over mountain waves

rc-nacreous-light.text: Mother-of-pearl irisation and an orange to pink afterglow, strongest once the sun is down and outlasting the cirrus beneath after dusk.
behaviors: Visible only once the sun is a few degrees below the horizon
Brightest while the sun is several degrees down; bright after the cirrus beneath has greyed, and outlasts it after dusk
signals: iridescent colour on a sky already dark
pastel colours against the sunset afterglow

sg-sighting-search.term: finding a lenticular or noctilucent sighting
sg-sighting-search.text: A lens stood over a ridge, or a faint streak on deep blue with stars still showing. The hour is open: the lenticular sources give no time of day.
behaviors: The lens holds still while the air passes through it
For a noctilucent, seen once the sun is a few degrees below the horizon
For a noctilucent, brightest when edge-on to the observer
sg-sighting-search.principle: The still shape or the lit streak is the sighting; the wind or the dark sky around it is what the reader infers.

lexicon._about: Brain-dump vocabulary around clouds, rarity and haiku: words, moods, adjacent concepts, lineage and search phrases. Seed material and options, not a set to copy. Cloud names live in cloud_types and cloud_words.

lx-register-technical.text: Terms a meteorologist or observer uses for cloud form, height and optics.

cw-aki-no-yuugure.text: Autumn dusk or autumn evening twilight, a favored haiku image linked with the passing of time.
signals: the sun sinking quickly into twilight

cw-yakoun.text: Noctilucent cloud, a dictionary gloss seen in a search result only. No fetched source gives its season; check a saijiki before using it as kigo.

cw-iwashigumo.text: Cirrocumulus, called mackerel sky; a search snippet listed it as an autumn word. Not confirmed in fetched text. Check a standard saijiki before using it.

worn_paths._about: What a model writes from only 'a haiku about rare clouds'. Worn paths are the easiest lines to write, so the reader has seen them before. Each one has a fresher move as an option.

wp-noise.text: Words that add no image to a haiku; each one can be replaced by the thing seen.

wp-overview.term: worn paths for a rare-cloud haiku
wp-overview.text: The generic haiku reaches for a soft white cloud, a mood word, a moral at the end, and the word rare said outright.
behaviors: A rare cloud named by its lens shape or edge colour sounds specific; a soft cloud sounds like any cloud
A last line that interprets the image closes the reader's part
wp-overview.principle: The worn path is the line a reader has already read a hundred times.
signals: fluffy or cotton in line one
the word rare in line two
